extraction_text: The narrator (Vaishampayana) concludes this as Chapter 3 of the Bhishma Parva in the Mahabharata.
Vaishampayana begins Chapter 4, noting that after hearing his son Dhritarashtra's words...
Vyasa (the sage poet) enters deep meditation to contemplate the supreme essence.
Vyasa, the great ascetic and philosopher of time, addresses Dhritarashtra, calling him 'Indra among kings'.
Vyasa explains that Time destroys and creates the world, and nothing is eternal. He urges Dhritarashtra to show the path of righteousness to the Kauravas and their allies.

attributes.supernatural_element: Concept of Time as a destructive/creative force

extraction_text: Vyasa warns that killing kin is vile and that Time has taken the form of Dhritarashtra's sons. He states that destroying family dharma destroys oneself.

Vyasa tells Dhritarashtra that the disaster taking the form of the kingdom brings misfortune, destroys the family and kings. He urges him to abandon it, regain his senses, and show his sons the path of dharma.
Vyasa concludes by advising Dhritarashtra to protect honor, dharma, and fame to attain heaven, let the Pandavas have the kingdom, and let the Kauravas have peace.

attributes.proposed_resolution: Pandavas get kingdom, Kauravas get peace

extraction_text: After Vyasa speaks, Dhritarashtra, the eloquent son of Ambika, begins to speak.
Dhritarashtra acknowledges that both he and Vyasa know about birth and death, but people are confused by their own interests, and he is an ordinary man.
Dhritarashtra praises Vyasa as powerful, gracious, their savior and guide, and says the Kauravas are not under his control, so Vyasa should not blame him.
Dhritarashtra honors Vyasa as dharma, auspiciousness, honor, fame, steadfastness, tradition, and the grandfather respected by both Kauravas and Pandavas.

attributes.relationship: Vyasa as grandfather to both clans

extraction_text: Vyasa tells Dhritarashtra to speak his mind, and he will dispel his doubts.
Dhritarashtra says he wishes to hear truthfully about all the characteristics of the victorious side in war.

Vyasa describes numerous omens of victory: pure sacrificial fire with upward flame, deep drum sounds, clear sun and moon, auspicious bird behaviors, well-adorned armies, cheerful warriors, favorable winds, and pure sensory experiences.
Vyasa states that whether large or small, troops that are excited and joyful are the sole标志 of victory, while the characteristics of the doomed are opposite.
One person's panic causes the entire army to panic, and even brave soldiers follow this panic.
The collapsing army is difficult to stop, compared to rushing water and frightened deer herds.

attributes.description: Unstoppable retreat

extraction_text: The army retreats uncontrollably; seeing panicked deserters makes brave warriors panic, increasing the terror.
The army collapses and flees in all directions; even warriors cannot stop it.
A wise king stands firm and tries to stabilize the four armies.
It is said that winning by cleverness is best, by division is moderate, and by war is worst; war brings great harm and death.
With mutual understanding, cheerful mood, and unwavering determination, fifty such warriors can crush an army; five, six, or seven unyielding warriors can achieve victory.
Garuda, son of Vinata, does not seek help from the masses even when seeing flocks of Garudas.
Large numbers do not guarantee victory; victory is not fixed but depends on divine will; even winning in war leads to destruction.
This concludes Chapter 4 of the Bhishma Parva in the Mahabharata.
